articles.title: Tariffs Part 2: Electric Boogaloo
articles.summary: Tariffs 101 for those who do not know what it is
articles.body:
In a surprising turn of events, the Trump administration has announced that more tariffs are incoming. The US Trade Representative's office [proposed tariffs on 14 trading partners](https://www.ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/november/ustr-makes-determinations-and-proposes-actions-14-section-301-investigations-relating-structural) including China and Singapore, despite President Trump just meeting our respective leaders, President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, just about a week ago. What does this bode for us? 

Let us go through what a tariff is, and who pays for it. A tariff is a tax on goods imported into a country. Hence, when a Singapore-made product arrives in the US, it is the American company importing it that pays the tax at the border, not the Singapore government nor the Singapore-based seller (despite what many people believe). The importer then has a choice on whether he wants to absorb the tax, asks for discounts from the Singapore supplier, or pass the cost to its customers. They could also do a mix so everyone takes part in contributing to the tariffs. 

This is not the first tariff we have seen. Remember last year's 'Liberation Day' when President Trump imposed sweeping tariffs across (his physical tariff) board? In February this year, the US Supreme Court [ruled](https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/02/supreme-court-strikes-down-tariffs/) that the President could not impose sweeping tariffs under an 'economic emergency law'. Since then, the US government has been finding ways to rebuild its tariffs using other trade laws.

Tariffs are imposed as a protectionist measure, meaning that the country deploys it as an attempt to protect domestic industries. So let's say if you are an American consumer, and you come across two similar products, one made in China and one made in the US, with them being priced at $10 and $12, respectively. If you are a price-sensitive consumer and find that you may not need the American-made one, more likely than not, you will purchase the Chinese-made one at a lower price. With tariffs of let's say... 20%, the Chinese-made good may now increase to $12, assuming the importer chooses to pass on all costs to the consumer. You may then feel compelled to purchase the American-made one, since they are now the same price. That is what tariffs do, they aim to protect domestic industries. 

Now, how would this affect you if you were the exporter. Well, American citizens may choose their domestically produced goods, reducing the demand of your product. This means less business coming from America, and less export revenue from the US. This could hurt your business. 

Ultimately, there is a lot of uncertainty, and this is still just a proposal, not final. Talks could continue and discussions are still ongoing, with hearings starting from 25 January. What should we watch? What goods get exempted, and whether Singapore can land a trade deal, we are still uncertain. Until then, there's no need to panic. Enjoy the year-end holidays, and keep watch on January.

articles.title: How Supply Shock from the Strait of Hormuz Moves into Supermarket Prices
articles.summary: This piece teaches those who are unsure about how macroeconomic events can translate into daily prices, through our real life example on the Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
This year, the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted, stalling deliveries in one of the most important trade routes in the world. You might be wondering how the price you pay for goods and services can be affected. The route has played an important part in allowing commodities such as oil, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fertiliser from the Gulf to pass through to the rest of the world.

Oil is one of the most important commodities in the world, if not the most important. It is a necessity in our daily lives such as in transport, power generation and cooking. LNG is also another important alternative energy source, especially for Singapore. Singapore relies on imported natural gas, as [about 95% of our electricity](https://ema.gov.sg/our-energy-story/energy-supply/natural-gas) is generated from the natural gas. When there is a shortage of either of these, it would result in prices creeping up, as everyone fights for the limited supply. 

At the same time, due to increased costs of oil, gas, fertiliser and more, these could further increase the price of end products for consumers. For example, I'm sure you have all experienced price markups at food stores, with them justifying that they had to pass on some increase in costs to the consumer. This is known as cost-push inflation.

That is how this disruption in the Strait of Hormuz could have caused prices to increase in our everyday lives. As I write this, I see that the data for the US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index has just been released, with them stating that [inflation has increased to 3.8%](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-october-2026) (year-on-year basis), up from 3.6% in September. With this increase, it is likely that the Federal Reserve, America's Central Bank, will impose an interest rate hike in December (estimated around 0.25 percentage points). This is known as contractionary monetary policy, where the bank increases interest rates to reduce spending and curb inflation.

This matters for us in Singapore as well. Higher US interest rates tend to increase borrowing costs worldwide (as interest rate is the cost of borrowing), and in Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) manages inflation through the exchange rate, by letting the Singapore dollar strengthen. 

Nonetheless, whether this interest rate hike can really curb inflation remains to be seen, as this time, inflation is caused by cost-push reasons, not demand-pull (where demand increases at a faster rate than supply). A rate hike cannot bring back the lost oil supply, though it can stop higher prices from spreading into other costs.

articles.title: 2026 in Markets: An Oil Shock, an AI Reckoning and a Sombre Finish
articles.summary: From the Iran war's oil shock to the sharp repricing of AI stocks, why markets are ending the year on edge, and what could bring relief
articles.body:
This year, we have seen extreme volatility in the markets, starting with oil prices spiking as the US and Israel [went to war with Iran](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/1/how-us-israel-attacks-on-iran-threaten-the-strait-of-hormuz-oil-markets). The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has caused lots of uncertainty and concern over stability of the world's most precious resource, with countries attempting to scramble and find alternative suppliers or look for other sources of energy. All of this has led to a supply shock that pushed energy prices and inflation all around the world.

At the same time, we saw the AI market boom as technology and AI-related stocks soared in price, with high corporate earnings being announced and chip supply sold out well into 2027. However, reality hit in the last quarter of 2026 as we see stock prices fall just as sharply as they rose earlier in the year. Many investors were caught off guard, and regulators in Korea, Taiwan and China [had to step in](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/11/6/tech-stock-rout-driven-by-us-ai-fears-continues-in-asian-trading) to calm the market players and supported buying. Large repricing of technology stocks amid exorbitant valuations will likely continue until the market is convinced it has found fair value.

While we are nearing the end of 2026, it seems like the year will end on a sombre note for market participants, especially those who are still holding onto the technology stocks that fell dramatically from their all-time high. With expectations of inflation picking up and interest rates rising in December, there is a lot of uncertainty in the market. Furthermore, as a blue wave hit the US Congress, with AI being a [key campaign issue](https://time.com/article/2026/11/04/midterm-elections-results-ai-industry-data-centers/), tensions and gridlock between the Democratic Congress and the White House could potentially put more pressure on the stock market.

Some signs of relief could come from:

1. A lasting US-Iran deal and a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz
2. Clarity on the Democratic Party's goals going forward
3. Earnings that could convince investors that AI is indeed here to stay in the long run

articles.title: The Singapore Instability
articles.summary: Macroeconomic concerns have caused global uncertainty. As such, what can Singaporeans expect, and how should we prepare for it?
articles.body:
In recent times, global instability has become more prevalent. Just to preface, this is not an outlook on the stock market, but we look at the impact of energy shocks, tariffs, and high interest rates on the average consumer in Singapore, and what we can do about it. This piece argues that the real risk is not a sudden crash, but a slow squeeze on our budgets, job security, and a few other issues that could gradually but quietly erode  our economy and wellbeing.

On 24 November 2026, the Singaporean government raised its forecast for the country's 2026 growth to be around 6% (Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry [METI], 2026b). That sounds great, especially for a mature economy, and this is in spite of the issues being faced in the Middle East, US tariffs, and persistent American inflation. With such good-sounding numbers, why is it still a cause for concern? Well, most of the growth this year has come from the AI-related chip and electronics industries, while consumer-facing businesses have been weaker (Monetary Authority of Singapore [MAS], 2026). Retrenchments in Singapore have also increased (Ministry of Manpower [MOM], 2026), and every other day, I see online comments and posts about a battered Singapore job market. 

To calculate a country's 'growth', the general consensus is to use its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as a proxy. On a slightly more technical side, the formula to calculate GDP is: Consumption + Investment + Government Expenditure + Exports - Imports (those who have learned economics will recall **GDP = C+I+G+(X-M)**). Generally, 'good' growth numbers tend to be around 2-4% per year for advanced economies, meaning that a 6% growth sounds like the country did fantastic. The concern is that growth is narrow, and it is largely dependent on one booming industry while other sectors are softer.



## Persistent Shocks

1. Strait of Hormuz: The disruption in the world's most important shipping route, carrying about a fifth of the world's oil supply (U.S. Energy Information Administration [EIA], 2026) has caused Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, to spike as high as US$126 a barrel at the end of April (Euronews, 2026), and it went above US$100 again in October. Although it fell to about US$89 on 24 November (Reuters, 2026a), it jumped back above US$93 the very next day after Yemen's Houthis claimed a drone attack on a Saudi refinery (Reuters, 2026b), which shows how every new attack in the region can send it back up.
2. Tariffs: In 2025, US President Donald Trump announced 'Liberation Day', where he imposed sweeping tariffs on the US's trading partners (if you do not know what a tariff is, read my opinion post [here](https://limzhbryan.github.io/#article-tariffs-part-2-electric-boogaloo)). On 25 November 2026, the US proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, including Singapore at up to 20% (Office of the United States Trade Representative [USTR], 2026). While nothing takes effect until after January, this has caused instability and uncertainty in our economy.
3. Interest-Rate Hikes: The US core inflation, measured by the Federal Reserve's preferred Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index rose to 3.3% in October (U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis [BEA], 2026), and markets now expect a rate-hike in December. As interest rates are the costs of borrowing, it may dampen buying and investments sentiment (think of yourself taking a loan to purchase a house or car, it becomes more expensive if interest rates are high).
4. AI and tech cycle: AI investment is the reason that Singapore's growth looks so strong. However, the MAS expects such activities to moderate in the second half of 2027. The concern is a sharp pullback, which we observe in recent times, reflected by the sharp decline in stock prices for technology companies.

While these shocks may seem manageable on its own, a combination or culmination of all these factors could create more instability and uncertainty in the Singapore economy.



## Prices

Singapore imports more than 90% of our food (Singapore Food Agency [SFA], 2026), and about 95% of our electricity is generated from imported natural gas (Energy Market Authority [EMA], 2025). This means that we are more vulnerable to imported inflation. When the price of oil or gas jumps overseas, it trickles down into our economy a few months later in the form of electricity bills, cost of goods in supermarkets, or taxi fares. For now, the numbers look tame as headline inflation fell to 1.9% in October, and core inflation (which excludes private transport and accommodation), eased to 1.5% (METI, 2026a). Electricity tariffs for October to December were cut by 10.4%, which means that a typical 4-room HDB household saves around $13 a month before GST as oil was cheaper over the summer (SP Group, 2026).

However, I would not get too comfortable, as SP Group has already warned that tariffs could rise again next quarter since fuel prices have climbed since September (AsiaOne, 2026). The MAS also said that risks to inflation are "tilted to the upside" and they expect inflation to stay slightly elevated in the coming months (MAS,2026). With the repeated energy shocks going on, the spike doesn't come at one go, but comes in a series of waves, where we observe bills going up, easing, and going up again.

The MAS manages exchange rate rather than interest rates through the $NEER (Singapore dollar Nominal Effective Exchange Rate, the trade-weighted value of the Singapore dollar against a basket of major trading partners' currencies). This policy enables the Singapore dollar to strengthen gradually against our trading partners' currencies, which helps make our imports cheaper and takes out some of the pain from global price rises. This is a big reason why our core inflation has stayed below America's 3.3% (caveat, our countries measure it differently).



## Jobs and wages

On paper, our job market looks fine, with overall unemployment being around 2.0% in September, and employment grew by 27,700 in the third quarter (MOM, 2026). However, when we look deeper, it seems less convincing than it seems. The resident unemployment rate edged up to 3.0%, and retrenchments rose to 4,800. The MOM describes "emerging weaknesses in parts of the labour market". The layoffs are concentrated in "outward-oriented sectors" such as information and communications, financial services and manufacturing. These are the industries that are more vulnerable to the aforementioned persistent shocks. Tech and finance companies are reorganising as they invest more in AI and cut costs. Furthermore, the uncertainty of further tariffs has made firms uncertain on what to expect in the near future.

Most new jobs for residents are coming from essential and public services (MOM, 2026). This shows that the economy is not exactly collapsing, but we see a structural shift. The state of the labour market in Singapore now seems to be that the concern is not about mass unemployment, but about slowing pay rises, fewer openings in better-paid sectors, and potentially longer job searches.



## How to prepare

Now with so much uncertainty looming, how can you better prepare yourself for uncertainty:

1. Build a bigger cash buffer: Build at least three to six months of expenses. With higher retrenchment, I would recommend six, especially if you work in tech, finance or manufacturing.
2. Up-skilling: With shifting trends in employment, it is important for you to up-skill yourself to keep up with changing times. The Singapore government has always been an advocate for up-skilling, with initiatives through SkillsFuture.
3. Networking: Join communities to speak and hear about other people’s experiences. Perhaps you could make a friend who might be able to find job opportunities that might suit you!

## Final Remarks

There are limits to what I post, as Singapore could be fine or better than fine. If the Hormuz disruption eases and oil continues to fall, inflation could drop sharply. Tariffs could be negotiated, and the AI boom may last longer than expected. Nonetheless, all of these are just basic analyses and they imagine a negative picture in the near term. Ultimately, most of what happens would depend on what the US does next. A clearer picture could be seen when the Democrats officially enters Congress in January next year. 



Once again, this basis analysis shares my own opinion and should not be taken as financial advice.

articles.title: Singapore's LNG Balance
articles.summary: How much LNG will Singapore need as demand grows and our pipeline contracts end, and is our terminal ready for it?
articles.body:
About 95% of Singapore's electricity comes from natural gas, and we import all of it (Energy Market Authority [EMA], 2026b). This year, Middle East tensions and an 18-day cut in piped gas from Indonesia have highlighted some vulnerability in our import-dependent energy mix. While Singapore keeps fuel stockpiles (their size is not disclosed) and intends to invest in energy storage capabilities (Singapore Economic Development Board [EDB], 2026), it will take some time before we can reduce our reliance on imported gas. Hence, I built a simple model of Singapore's gas balance. Based on my model, if Indonesia stops piping gas to us after its contracts end in 2028, our only LNG terminal could be around 90% to 100% full in 2029, a year before the second terminal opens.



## Our Gas Usage

We need to highlight how our gas is being used. The obvious one is power, and we can use EMA's forecast of Singapore's electricity generation to have an understanding of how our power usage will grow in the coming years, and analyse whether our supply is sufficient. The EMA forecasts that Singapore's electricity generation will grow from 60.1 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025 to 67.6 TWh by 2030 in the base case (EMA, 2025).



## Origin of Imports

Singapore gets its gas in two ways, through pipelines or through shipments of liquefied natural gas (LNG). In 2025, 43% of our gas was supplied through pipelines from Malaysia and Indonesia, while the remaining 57% was supplied as LNG, gas chilled to a liquid state so that it can be shipped by tanker (RecordOwl, 2026).

Pipelines are the cheap and steady base, as the infrastructure is already in place, and they are not vulnerable to tanker supply or freight cost volatility. LNG, however, is a flexible top-up option to fill whatever gap the pipelines are not able to supply. Hence, this analysis piece aims to look at the supply-demand balance in Singapore, as our demand for electricity increases and as we attempt to reduce our reliance on individual countries.

We can analyse it through the following model:

LNG required = gas for power + gas for industry - pipeline gas supply

![Bar chart: Singapore gas supply by source in 2025 and in 2029 if Indonesia stops](/files/charts/lng-supply-mix.svg)

*Source: my estimates, based on EMA (2025), RecordOwl (2026) and US EIA data via Agence France-Presse [AFP] (2026).*



## Need for Diversification

While we do have contractual agreements with our neighbours Malaysia and Indonesia, it is essential for us to understand that tensions can potentially cause issues in our power generation.

In October 2026, the timing of the 18-day supply cut from Indonesia raised questions. Smoke from Indonesia's most intense forest fires in 11 years had drifted over Singapore, Malaysia and Timor-Leste, and Singapore promised legal action against the companies responsible (The Star, 2026a; AFP, 2026). Days later, Indonesia cut pipeline gas to Singapore, stating that it was to protect gas supply for its own power plants, and Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia told Singapore not to lecture Indonesia on honouring contracts (AFP, 2026; Tanamal & Karyza, 2026).

Tensions have since cooled, with the two foreign ministers meeting in Jakarta in late October and discussing a joint task force on the fires, with Singapore offering to share data on companies linked to the burning (The Star, 2026a). Despite this, it shows how important it is for Singapore to look for alternative sources of supply, as we are still highly dependent on pipeline gas from two countries and any issues arising between Singapore and its suppliers could put Singapore's energy supply at risk. Singapore's two pipeline contracts with Indonesia (about 30% of our gas) are slated to end in 2028. While Singapore's contracts with Malaysia (about 10% to 12% of our gas) do not have a public end date, some of them are shorter contracts of under five years, which could end sooner (Ho, 2026). As such, it is imperative that Singapore understands its own LNG supply balance, and looks at where it could diversify its supplier portfolio.



## Possible Worsening Scenarios

### 1. Indonesia Ends Its Contracts

Indonesia's energy minister said that he is considering not renewing gas export contracts with neighbouring countries (Malay Mail, 2026). If the contracts lapse, about 410 billion British thermal units per day (BBTUD, the official unit EMA uses for gas) will disappear in 2029. This could lead to serious repercussions, especially considering EMA's estimation of increased electricity generation in Singapore. Based on my model, our LNG needs would jump from about 5.4 to 8.3 million tonnes (Mt) a year, and LNG would make up almost 90% of our gas.

### 2. Data-Centre Boom

EMA forecasted that there could be an increase in data centres and advanced manufacturing, potentially requiring electricity generation of up to 80.4 TWh by 2030 (EMA, 2025). If that does come to pass, our LNG needs would climb to about 7.0 Mt by 2030. When we combine this with the scenario in which Indonesia ends its contracts, our current LNG terminal capacity will not be enough.

### 3. Another Gulf Shock

Before the war, Qatar sent about one LNG cargo a month to Singapore, which ends up being about 10% of our total gas demand (Hellenic Shipping News, 2026). If this issue persists and we continue to lose Qatari cargoes and replace them with spot cargoes, the extra costs may trickle down and cause electricity prices to rise. Based on my model, losing a year of Qatari cargoes and buying spot cargoes instead could cost us an extra S$410 million to S$970 million, depending on spot prices.

All of these point to potential concerns in our LNG supply in 2029 if Indonesia chooses to cut its gas supply to us, and our second LNG terminal is not yet ready.

![Line chart: LNG Singapore needs by scenario against terminal room, 2025 to 2030](/files/charts/lng-scenarios.svg)

*Source: my estimates, based on EMA (2025, 2026b) and Singapore LNG Corporation (2025). Terminal room is peak capacity less reloads and ship fuel.*



## Is Singapore Ready?

Singapore acknowledges that we are heavily reliant on imported gas. As such, the country has been investing heavily in infrastructure and facilities to increase LNG supply. In October, EMA set out a five-year plan (EMA, 2026b).

- **More LNG capacity:** A second LNG terminal at Jurong Port will increase import capacity to 15 Mt a year by 2030. EMA is also studying the possibility of expanding the first terminal on Jurong Island, and possibly establishing a new energy cluster with another LNG terminal on Pulau Tekong.
- **Improved gas efficiency:** New gas-fired plants will come online from now till 2031. This raises our generation capacity by about 26% from 12 GW today. These new plants must also be able to run partly on hydrogen, with the option to switch fully to hydrogen later (EMA, 2023). As these newer plants are more efficient and burn less gas per unit of power, they could slow the growth in our LNG needs.
- **Less reliance on gas:** Singapore has been finding ways to utilise other sources of energy for our electricity generation. For instance, we are adding more solar power, and studying a second power link to import electricity from Malaysia.
- **Stronger grids and centralised purchase:** Singapore plans to invest up to S$5.3 billion to expand our power grid between 2025 and 2029 (EDB, 2026). Singapore has also set up a national gas company, Singapore GasCo, in 2025 (Malay Mail, 2026), and EMA plans for one supplier to buy gas for the whole power sector (EMA, 2026a). Buying as a sole purchaser could give Singapore more negotiating power for cargoes.

Most of these steps aim to increase our volume and reliability, with the second terminal's timing being the one to watch, as our troubles could come by 2029. The investments in new gas plants, while more efficient, imply that Singapore aims to lock in gas as the backbone of our power generation. Still, our troubles could lessen if Jakarta agrees on a price to export electricity to us, as Singapore plans to import up to 3.4 GW of low-carbon power from Indonesia by 2035 (The Star, 2026b). These new investments improve our resilience, but do not take away our exposure to the global LNG market.



## Closing Remarks

Based on calculations, if Indonesian gas stops in 2029, our one terminal would be around 90% to 100% full once we count reloads and ship fuel, depending on whether we use its peak capacity of 11 Mt (Singapore LNG Corporation, 2025) or the 10 Mt that EMA gives (EMA, 2026b). That is a year before the second terminal at Jurong Port increases capacity to 15 Mt (EMA, 2026b). The Singapore LNG (SLNG) average capacity is lower than its peak, about 9 Mt a year (Singapore LNG Corporation, 2025). Hence, the squeeze is real. Any delay to our second terminal or an early end to the Indonesian supply would be troubling for Singapore's power generation.

The price exposure is also a real risk. In my model, every US$1 increase in the LNG price costs Singapore about US$280 million a year. Thus, losing Indonesian gas would not just cause us issues in shorter supply, but also raise costs that could potentially trickle down to the economy.

The 2026 shocks were relatively manageable so far, as they were either small or short. The Indonesian cut was less than 2% of our daily demand (RecordOwl, 2026) and EMA found replacement cargoes for Qatar's, such as from the US, Australia and Africa (Hellenic Shipping News, 2026). A permanent loss of pipeline gas in 2029 is a different kind of risk, however, as it is long lasting.

The caveat in this piece is that it is a simple model. Contract prices are confidential, so my model uses estimates and the numbers may not truly reflect real life. Nonetheless, the direction is clear. So what should we watch? First, whether Indonesia renews its contracts before they end in 2028. Second, whether the second terminal at Jurong Port is ready on time. Third, spot LNG prices, as they decide how much extra we pay whenever supply is disrupted.
